opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I'm pretty skeptical of that objection, for a few reasons.

First, "reason" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and people rarely define it. If you mean something like "can take a novel problem, break it into steps, apply general principles, and reach a correct conclusion it hasn't seen before," then current systems clearly do that some of the time. Not perfectly or reliably, but neither do humans. If you mean something stricter, like executing a sound logical procedure with guarantees, then humans mostly don't reason by that standard either. We use heuristics, pattern matching, and analogy, and we make systematic errors. So the bar often gets set in a way that, applied consistently, would rule out human reasoning too.

Second, there's a recurring pattern where someone says "these systems can't do X, therefore they're not really reasoning," then a year or two later the models do X, and the goalposts move. I don't think that's always bad faith. It's hard to articulate what you think intelligence is until you see something that's almost but not quite it. But it should make us humble about confident claims of fundamental limitations.

Third, even if you grant that today's models have real gaps, like brittle out-of-distribution generalization, trouble with long-horizon planning, or confabulation, that's an argument about the current state of the art, not about what's achievable this century. "This century" is seventy-plus years. Compare where the field was in 2012 with where it is now. To get from "current systems can't reason well" to "we won't get AGI by 2100," you'd need a much stronger claim: that there's some principled barrier the whole research program can't get past. I haven't seen a convincing argument for that.

There's also the mechanistic angle, which is closer to what I work on. When you look inside these models, you find structured internal representations and computations that look a lot more like algorithms than lookup tables. That doesn't settle the philosophical question, but it cuts against the "it's just memorizing surface statistics" story that often motivates the objection.

So I'd say the "can't reason" objection is a useful prompt for figuring out where current models fail and why. As an argument against AGI this century, it's weak. If anything, I'd worry more about people being overconfident in the other direction, assuming it's all imminent and straightforward. The honest position is a lot of uncertainty, and not much of that uncertainty comes from a deep "machines can't reason" barrier.

r001.rationale: It says whether current systems reason depends on what “reason” means, then gives examples under different definitions.

r002.rationale: It argues that current gaps do not establish a barrier to AGI this century, but does not address a new architecture or paradigm for system-two reasoning.

r003.rationale: It calls the objection weak and notes AGI could arrive this century, but does not say that this timeline warrants substantial attention now.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the claim is doing a lot less work than people want it to do. When someone says "current systems can't reason," I always want to ask what they mean by reason, because usually they have in mind something like a crisp, symbolic, step-by-step process that's guaranteed to be correct. And by that standard, humans don't reason either. Most of what we do is fast, heuristic, pattern-matched, and then we tell ourselves a tidy story afterwards. There's a huge literature in cognitive science on this. So if the objection is "these models are just doing sophisticated pattern matching," my response is, well, yes, and so are you, and the question is whether the patterns are general enough to get the job done.

Then there's the empirical side. Every time someone draws a line and says "a real reasoner could do X and these models can't," that line tends to get crossed within a year or two. We saw this with arithmetic, with multi-step planning, with code, with the whole chain-of-thought and reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks paradigm that made the models dramatically better at long-horizon math and programming problems. The failures that remain are real, I'm not dismissing them, they're brittle in weird ways, they still get fooled by surface features. But the trend is not that we're hitting a ceiling. The trend is that the failure modes keep shrinking as we scale and as we train directly on the thing we care about.

I'd also separate two different claims that get run together. One is "today's models can't reason," which is at best half true depending on your definition. The other is "nothing in this paradigm could ever reason, so AGI is far off." That second claim is the one you'd need for the objection to work, and I just don't see the argument for it. You'd have to believe there's some ingredient in biological brains that gradient descent on large neural networks fundamentally can't recover, and nobody has actually identified that ingredient. Every candidate that's been proposed, symbol manipulation, compositionality, world models, has turned out to be something these systems acquire to some degree when you give them enough data and the right training signal.

So my honest assessment is that the "can't reason" objection is mostly a bet that the current trajectory stalls out, dressed up as a conceptual argument. It might stall out! I'm not certain about timelines, and I think people who confidently say three years are overreaching. But "this century" is a very long time, and the reasoning objection in particular is one of the weakest reasons to be skeptical of that.

r001.rationale: The response says whether current systems can reason depends on what someone means by “reason,” and gives a definition-based distinction.

r002.rationale: It argues that the current paradigm may develop reasoning and that the objection to AGI this century is weak, but does not address whether a new architecture or paradigm for system-two reasoning would be unlikely to delay AGI beyond 2100.

r003.rationale: It describes this century as a long time and the reasoning objection as weak, but does not say that AGI by 2100 is soon enough to warrant substantial attention now.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think that’s a very strong objection. You can debate whether what current systems do deserves to be called reasoning, but even if we grant that they can’t reason, that doesn’t establish that we won’t build systems that can sometime this century. That’s a claim about the trajectory of research, not just the capabilities of today’s models.

And I think the premise is too categorical. These systems can solve some problems that require combining information and taking multiple steps. They also fail in surprising ways. That suggests their reasoning is unreliable or limited, rather than completely absent. We should ask which problems they can solve, how reliably, and whether those limitations are improving—not treat reasoning as a single switch that’s either on or off.

You could argue that some limitation requires a fundamentally different approach. But then you need an argument for why we won’t discover that approach over the next several decades. Pointing to a failure in a current model doesn’t get you there.

r001.rationale: The response says whether current systems count as reasoning depends on what we mean by “reasoning.”

r002.rationale: It argues that even if a fundamentally different approach is needed, we may discover it over the next several decades, so that need does not establish that AGI will arrive after this century.

r003.rationale: The response discusses whether AGI may arrive this century but does not say that this possibility warrants substantial attention now.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a pretty weak objection to AGI this century, because even if you grant the premise, it doesn’t establish that the limitation will persist. A hundred years is a long time to improve these systems.

But I’d also push back on the premise. What do we mean by reasoning? If we mean combining information to solve a problem that you haven’t encountered before, current systems seem to do at least some of that. They’re unreliable, and they can fail on things that look very simple to us, but that’s different from saying they cannot reason at all. Humans are also quite sensitive to how a problem is presented.

The more interesting question is what explains the failures. Are we seeing a fundamental limitation of the approach, or something that can improve with better training, more computation at inference time, or access to tools? You need an argument for why those routes won’t work. Just pointing to a failure in a current model doesn’t give you that.

r001.rationale: The response asks what “reasoning” means and says current systems can do at least some reasoning under one definition, making the assessment partly dependent on the definition.

r002.rationale: It says a century leaves time for improvement, but does not address whether needing a new architecture or paradigm for system-two reasoning would delay AGI beyond 2100.

r003.rationale: It calls the objection weak, but does not say that AGI by 2100 would be soon enough to warrant substantial attention now.
